Offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.

These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.

Where to start: a practical implementation plan

I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.

  1. Preserve the evidence. Confirm that raw values, units, source identifiers, measurement timestamps, arrival timestamps, and relevant metadata are captured before transformation.
  2. Define the temporal contract. Document how observations are aligned, how stale data is handled, and what happens when a required measurement is missing or late.
  3. Make coordinate assumptions explicit. Identify which calculations depend on phone orientation, how transformations are established, and how uncertainty affects downstream use.
  4. Introduce a quality contract. Define accept, degrade, and abstain outcomes for one event type. Record reason codes so that quality failures can be distinguished from event-rule failures.
  5. Validate failure scenarios. Test delayed, missing, duplicated, out-of-order, and contradictory observations. Test phone rotations and changes in sensor availability, not only normal journeys.
  6. Instrument the pipeline. Track timestamp skew, data freshness, sampling gaps, quality outcomes, event revisions, and end-to-end latency.
  7. Expand incrementally. Once the chosen event has a defensible processing path, apply the same architectural contracts to other event types, adapting the quality requirements to each use case.

The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.

What this architecture does not solve

A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.

It cannot recover missing evidence

The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.

It does not replace algorithm validation

The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.

Quality thresholds are not universal

Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.

Operational trade-offs remain

Background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.

Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.

Conclusion: reliability belongs to the pipeline

Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.

The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.

The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.

The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

entries.title: Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window
entries.summary: Mozilla has partnered with Mistral AI to offer Mistral Small 4, an open-weight model, in Firefox's Smart Window AI assistant, now in beta. It is recommended for users in France, the US and Canada. Users can choose among several models, and Mistral agreed to zero data retention. Beta feedback is mixed. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
Mozilla, the non-profit organisation behind the Firefox browser, has announced a partnership with Paris-based Mistral AI to bring the French company's open-weight models into Firefox Smart Window, Mozilla's AI browsing assistant currently in beta.

The deal introduces Mistral Small 4 as a recommended model for Smart Window users in France, the United States and Canada, with rollouts planned for the United Kingdom and Germany later this year. It coincides with Smart Window's first expansion beyond North America and marks a deliberate attempt by Mozilla to resist the pattern of browser makers coupling tightly to a single American AI provider.

Smart Window, originally announced in November 2025 as "AI Window", operates as an optional window separate from regular browsing. It helps users make sense of complex searches, group related tabs, revisit pages they have seen before and carry work across sessions. Users decide when to use it, which model to use and what browsing context to share. Conversations are not stored on Mozilla's servers by default, and Mistral has agreed to zero data retention for the partnership.

Mistral Small 4 is a 119-billion-parameter model distributed on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence. Mozilla selected it after evaluating performance in the beta, with multilingual quality as a central criterion. According to Cybernews, the partnership expands Mistral's reach by approximately 200,000 active monthly Firefox users, giving the French company its first large consumer distribution channel outside its own Le Chat app.

Mozilla Corporation CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo framed the deal as a bet on openness: "A browser shouldn't be a one-way funnel. It should preserve what made the internet powerful to begin with: the freedom to explore, discover different ideas and tech, and decide for ourselves where to go next." Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch described the collaboration as "two open source advocates working together."

The move puts Firefox alongside, but distinct from, Chrome's Gemini integration, Edge's Copilot sidebar and Opera's Aria. Where those tightly couple the browser to one vendor's stack, Smart Window's picker lets users switch between Gemini, Qwen, Mistral Small 4 and others. Golem.de highlighted this multi-model approach as Mozilla's strategic differentiator against the single-provider lock-in of its larger rivals.

Reception on Mozilla Connect, where the project gathers beta feedback, has been mixed. Some testers have praised the privacy controls, while others question whether Mozilla should be investing in AI at all. One commenter argued that remaining "AI-free would set you apart and draw in a demographic desperate to be catered to." Others reported practical frustrations, including theming inconsistencies with vertical tabs, bookmarks that fail to carry over from Classic Windows and a mandatory Mozilla account login that erodes trust from the outset.

For Firefox users wanting to try Smart Window, access is handled through the waitlist at firefox.com/smart-window. Once invited, the feature can also be toggled through the browser.smartwindow.enabled preference, with configuration guidance in Mozilla's about:config documentation. Firefox 155 introduced French-language support, and Mistral Small 4 appears under the Personalised category in Smart Window's model picker.

Firefox is Mozilla's open-source browser, maintained since 2004 by Mozilla Corporation. Mistral AI, founded in 2023 in Paris, publishes open-weight language models with a focus on European languages and regulatory contexts.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review
entries.summary: Ankit Jain of Aviator told QCon San Francisco 2026 that line-by-line code review is already fading, since most review comments concern knowledge sharing rather than defects and over 75% of PRs merge without human review. He proposed six layers: argue, capture, codify, prove, debate, own. His team merges four times more PRs, with about 40% fewer reverts. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a company that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me."

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain said the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been."

A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain said, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

He closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

entries.title: Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills Through SRE-based Training
entries.summary: Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. We can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself. By Ben Linders
entries.content:
Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. In her talk, Engineer Confidence with Reliable Training Programs at GOTO Copenhagen, Jennifer Petoff showed how we can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself.

Software ownership is a human challenge as much as it is a technical one. Most formal education programs are geared towards the first 10% of the software development life cycle, the build phase, Petoff said. Engineers and operators are tasked with maintaining, debugging, securing, and evolving systems they may not even have written:

There’s this implicit assumption that coding proficiency translates seamlessly to operational confidence, but it doesn’t. Without systematic training, this may create imposter syndrome, stress, and maybe even attrition in your organization.

AI has magnified the relative cost and complexity of post-build operations. Petoff suggested thinking about how to equip developers and operators with skills to run their services scalably in production.

Culture is not some grand mindset you need to shift. It’s much more tactical. You can change your culture by changing what people do every day, Petoff said. Training people acts as a confidence engine, giving engineers the self-efficacy to adopt new operational behaviors. When behaviors are repeated over time and across teams, they become habits, and those habits comprise your organizational culture. Petoff suggests avoiding a sink-or-swim mentality (letting people fend for themselves rather than training them), as it can breed stress or frustration.

Training needs depend on the maturity of your organization in adopting key principles and practices, the familiarity of engineers with the organization and infrastructure, and the experience of individuals. For organizations starting their DevOps or SRE journey, she suggested addressing skill gaps and tailoring the message to who is on your team. Organizations that already have well-developed production best practices should aim at reinforcing their culture and building upon their practices to foster confidence.

Your training program should take into account the size of your organization and how fast it’s growing to get the most from your investment. If your organization is small and growing slowly, focus on one-on-one knowledge transfer through mentoring and shadowing, Petoff suggested. For a large and slowly growing organization, invest in ongoing education. When it’s small but growing rapidly, invest in onboarding. If you’re both large and growing rapidly, invest in a full life cycle training program, onboarding, all the way through ongoing education and beyond, she said.

The foundational principles of SRE and elements of the service reliability hierarchy can be applied to the training program itself, Petoff explained:

Monitor through attendance tracking and survey feedback. Address issues that surface via the monitoring. Write postmortems when something goes wrong to learn from that failure. Observe concrete job-related behaviors to more effectively tie the training to business impact.

To scale production safety training to tens of thousands of developers, they created a self-paced training and piloted it with a 1% cohort, making changes based on audience feedback before scaling it up. Petoff said they automated the distribution, enrollment, and escalation notifications up the management chain.

A production-ready workforce and organizational culture is non-negotiable in the generative AI era, Petoff stated. Learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and behavior repeated over time drives culture. You need to look at the training costs and benefits to make the right level of investment based on the specific organizational situation. Applying SRE principles to the training program itself led to a more consistent, reliable, and scalable experience, she concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Jennifer Petoff after her talk.

InfoQ: How can we tailor the training message to individual team members?

Jennifer Petoff: In the Generative AI era, we are all moving faster than ever, and it’s easy for training to get sacrificed as something important, but not urgent. Developers and operators may also look upon training with skepticism: Is this training tied to some fleeting corporate hype that will quickly be forgotten?

You need to convince them "what’s in it for me?" (WIIFM). The answer ties directly to what motivates people and varies among team members.

  • For the practically-minded: Tie the training to reductions in toil or on-call load.
  • For the growth-minded: Connect it to higher-value skills that can unlock career opportunities.
  • For people motivated by self-preservation: Explain how the training will build future-proof skills.

These "WIIFM" elements can be conveyed in written communications, through talking points to managers, or peer-to-peer discussions incorporated into the program.

InfoQ: How did you observe job-related behaviors?

Petoff: We built a hands-on training environment using real production infrastructure, but without real-world users and associated stakes. We could "break" our training infrastructure on demand, and students would work in groups of three to troubleshoot realistic production issues.

By structuring the training in this way, instructors could directly observe how participants used system diagrams, diagnosed production issues, and mitigated an outage. We looked at how people engaged with production during the exercises instead of quizzing them or asking for a simple nod of understanding.

InfoQ: What have you learned from applying SRE principles to training programs?

Petoff: Reliability is about mastering the operational "how" of any complex initiative. Training programs are just the tip of the iceberg. I believe that you can "SRE" anything in work, life, and for your well-being. Building is time-bound, but operations are forever. Planning a project beyond launch to include mechanisms to streamline operations and drive continuous improvement will pay you back tenfold and free up time to work on more impactful initiatives without getting buried under a mountain of toil.

entries.title: Presentation: Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell
entries.summary: Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge. By Rachel Shalom
entries.content:
Transcript

Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell. I'm part of a team that develops internal AI solutions for Dell. We develop solutions that basically Dell employees are using. I'm going to talk about some of the work we are doing inside Dell today. I'm actually going to start with the motivation of this talk. I'm leading an agentic search within Dell, a search system that searches for your information in internal sources like GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and other sources. Part of it is using semantic search, which is using also an embedding model. What we have noticed is that we keep failing in certain type of questions. Questions that have to do with internal terminology or questions that have to do with internal products of Dell. Here are some examples like PowerScale or CloudIQ or PowerProtect. These are the type of questions that are using internal terminology, or you can call it even internal language of Dell, that the system kept failing with retrieving the right answer. The motivation was, does the embedding model that is supposed to capture the meaning of those really understand the questions or the answers?

Outline

This is what we are going to talk about today. We'll discuss why embedding models are important and common training methodologies. We'll discuss also the common use cases for embeddings. I will talk about fine-tuning and a common loss function that is used today for training majority of the embedding models. We will talk about the use case at Dell more in depth and why we trained our own embedding model, discuss the data collection, and how did we evaluate and monitor the performance.

Why Embedding Models Are Important

Humans understand words, machines understand numbers. Embeddings is the bridge between them. Embedding is capturing the meaning of words and sentences. For example, you can see in that lane that in the embedding space, expressions that have to do with password or forgot my login or can't access account should be closer in the embedding space, while cities and countries will be in a different area in the embedding space, but closer to each other, and that's the meaning of representations. What are the common use cases for using embedding models? I think the most common one is information retrieval. Most of the companies or at least in the enterprise, you use RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation to retrieve information from a vector database. Classification is one more. For example, if you want to assign categories to your text, like you have incoming emails, the most trivial example is you want to target spam or not spam. Clustering is another very common use case for embedding models. If you want to make sense of your unstructured data, like you have incoming queries by customers and you want to group them together into clusters and recommendation systems to make personalized recommendations. There are probably others, but these are the most common ones.

How Are Embedding Models Trained?

Now I want to talk briefly on the general training procedures for embedding models. Usually when you train embedding models, you start with the first phase, which is the pre-training. Pre-training is done on what we call the chunk of the internet. You take everything that is available online, Wikipedia, books, public GitHub repository, anything you can imagine, and it's a lot of data, and it can be also junk data, but it's a lot of data that you put in. The way you train is by Masked Language Modeling, which means, as you see in the example, is that you give the model a sentence, each time you mask a different word, and then you let the model guess the word, and this is how you teach the model a general understanding of the language. A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.

At this stage, you really have to collect high-quality data. Usually it takes a long time, and it costs a lot of money normally. I'm going to talk about the preparation of what we call contrastive learning, which is a very common way to train or fine-tune embedding models nowadays. What you do normally is you prepare pairs or triplets of examples. For example, here, you have a question. Let's call it an anchor. How do I reset my password? Then you have a positive answer, which is how to reset it, and then you have a negative answer, which doesn't answer your question. The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. That's the goal of the fine-tuning, to take high-quality data and get the real semantic meaning for the text.

Training/Fine-Tuning: Loss Function

How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. If you take a look at different papers from Google or anyone else that is training embedding models, you will see different versions of the same loss function, but this is the basic one. If we go and see the batch, or we have let's say 100 examples of questions and answers, so if we take a look at a log expression, you will see that on the top we have the exponent of s is a cosine similarity between two vectors, the vector of the question and the vector of the positive answer. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.

All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. When you train an embedding model, the purpose is to bring up the similarity for positives and bring down the similarity for negatives. I added another slide for that just to maybe show it in a geometric way, so that you don't lose the context. Again, we have this log loss of positives versus negatives. If we take a look at the lower part, then you can see that if I have, let's say, a query, how do I reset my password? Then I have a positive question and a bunch of negative questions. Then, before training, you will see that the distance between the positive and negative vectors to the query are maybe, let's say, a little bit similar, and after training, you want to see that the positive answer is closer to the query, and the negatives are further away. I hope you at least enjoyed a little bit from this loss function. It's super beautiful.

Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Think about a model that is performing different tasks. Sometimes it is questions and answers. Sometimes it is clustering, as we mentioned before. Sometimes it is other tasks. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I think the answer would be it depends on the task. If we want to do clustering similarity between two sentences, then what is the capital of France, and number one would be more similar. If my task is to pair questions and answers, then what is the capital of France, and number two is more similar. In order to solve that, what is commonly done today when training with fine-tuning is to add prefixes.

As you can see, we have in orange the start clustering, what is the capital of France, and then clustering the answer, and that tells the model, please create vectors for clustering. They're going to get slightly different vectors because the task now is to say, these are two similar sentences. If I provide a different prefix, which is search_query, search_document, so the task is questions and answers. This is where you give the model a signal that we are now talking about a different task. This is one important thing to notice when training.

Use Case at Dell - A Multi-Agent System for Internal Search

I've talked a little bit about the use cases and a little bit generally about the training. Now let's talk about Dell, or what we did at Dell. We have an agentic search at Dell, which means we let R&D teams search within all of Dell's internal sources. For example, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, these are mostly relevant for engineers and product managers, SharePoint, also different databases. I'm going to talk about the architecture, but this is a hierarchical architecture of multiple agents that are making API calls. It also has a component of semantic search, which means we take all the data and ingest it in advance. It has a component of memory management, which is pretty common for agentic search applications. It's also permission aware, which is very important for any enterprise. These are some of the questions that we are getting normally, questions about bug solving, questions about onboarding to a new project, testing, technical configurations, procedural how-to.

We get all sorts of also weird questions, but these are the most common ones. This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself. We have the orchestrator, or what we call the supervisor, which is the entry point for every question. This is a router that routes the user question to any other of the agents. We have a GitHub agent, which means that it's a model with a set of tools, mainly API tools. We have a Confluence agent that is a model. They all have access, or it's access-based, to the information inside Dell. We have GitLab and GitHub, which is, again, exactly the same. Models with different API tools. We have security agent, which usually makes API calls to OSs like Ubuntu and SUSE, and provide CVE resolutions, and agents that are making database queries. Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.

We keep them that way in order to keep the context low and the context in place. We found it more effective that way. The supervisors can route the question to one or many agents. They return back an answer. The supervisor decides, do I want to go back to the user with an answer, or go back to the agents and bring another one? We, of course, limit the number of turns, so it won't take like one hour to get back to the user. This is how it works.

This is the general architecture of what we have. We have a web application. We are API first, which means there are other internal applications at Dell that are using this agentic search. It's a skill, and it is an MCP that is used within Windsurf and Claude Code. The backend, other than having this architecture that I explained before, it is using Langfuse for observability. This is an important part, Dell cares really about privacy. All of the data that we are having, it's highly restricted. We are mainly playing with open-source models, which means mostly it's running on-prem. Everything is running on-prem on Dell infrastructure. Recently, we started experimenting with Gemini and Sonnet, but in a very limited way. The whole system is around open source. Embedding, re-rankers, LLMs, and every time there is a new one, we are experimenting, but all of it is on-prem. There is another layer to this application, which is what we call auto data ingestion, or bring your own data there.

That is when someone wants to create their own bot, let's say, you just provide, here is a link to my Confluence or to my Jira, to my GitHub, and then it triggers a pipeline that does a lot of data plumbing, and ingest and chunk all the data, put it in a vector database, and it's ready for you to query. You can create your personal context space. A little bit more about the bring your own data architecture, it's important because this is the part that connects later to our embedding model, which is the main subject. If you have Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, we're taking all of the fields from Confluence, we take all the images and attachments, and so is for Jira. We do semantic chunks with code. We use AST, and we do a lot of cleanups, like these are too many details to talk about.

Then you might ask yourself, ok, so you do all of that job, but the rate of change is very high, so we update it every two days. We go and check with the APIs what were the changes, and then we re-embed all the changes every two days. Everything is saved in pgvector, which is, again, hosted on-prem, which I think is very nice that everything is hosted on-prem at Dell, that it's all private, nothing goes out. Just a little bit about chunking. I'm talking only on Confluence now because the work that we did in training the model, the context was Confluence. We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space, if you work with Confluence, you download thousands of pages, then we reformat it into HTML. We filter a lot of noise because there are a lot of emojis and stuff that are not relevant to the model, we turn it into an md file. We detect also tables to make sure that the context of the table is saved even when you chunk. We take all those attachments and then we chunk by paragraphs and use an embedding model and save it in a vector database. This is done for every request that we get and in advance.

Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place, we have lots of agents and we have also semantic search, now why fine-tune our own embedding? I started the lecture with saying that we saw gaps that the semantic search just didn't solve, and the gaps were mainly about questions on internal products, on abbreviations and acronyms that are specific to Dell, and workflows and processes, everything that is the Dell world or the Dell language, there are a lot of such data at Dell, that led us to think or to hypothesize that this is a reason for failure. Now when you run a RAG system, so there are potentially a lot of problems that could happen. It has a lot of stages and a lot of pieces moving around, so it could be something else. Our hypothesis said, let's try and see if we can improve the result by fine-tuning a model.

Generally speaking, I think that the signals you want to look for if you are planning a domain adaptation are to ask yourself like, is the data of the model out of the shelf that I'm taking on? Now I'm talking about models in the context of open source. We take most of the models from Hugging Face, normally you know what is the training data that they were trained on, you have leaderboards. You ask yourself, is the Dell data even similar to what those models were trained on? It can be that the terminology we use was used when this model was trained originally. These are the signs to look for when you want to train. There is another interesting thing to check. Again, every open-source model comes with a vocabulary. It's a list of tokens that the model has seen. This one was around 30,000. What happens when the model hasn't seen that word, they have a special token called unknown token.

That means the model said, I haven't seen that but I can manage, never mind. I put an unknown token. I wanted to understand how many unknown tokens do we have that the model completely hasn't seen at all? Not that it doesn't understand the semantics, it just didn't see those words. I was surprised to see that these are very general. I put here some examples that I saw, like Base64-encoded strings, or you can see Unicode box-drawing, all of these things that really have no meaning. It makes sense. All of the images, the model didn't recognize, that was surprising. I thought that models are trained on images now. Checkmarks and long camelCase compound words. This was a very small percentage of the data that the model didn't recognize. The reason I checked it is because when you fine-tune a model, I would like the model to semantically understand my data. If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning. That was a check. The check told me, it's fine. The model doesn't understand images. I don't care. Let's move on. We are continuing with fine-tuning.

Choosing the Base Model

One more thing to consider. How do you choose a base model? Open source now. Again, I work for an enterprise that cares about privacy a lot, so mostly open source running on-prem. The first thing that every company cares about is licensing and commercial usage, especially every large company like Dell. I am not allowed to touch any models the legal team hasn't approved. The second thing that I care about is how open is this model? When I say open, I'm not only talking about the model weights, but did they release the training code? Did they release the data that they trained on? This is very important. Then you look at benchmarks. When you look at benchmarks, I want to take a look at tasks that I care about. I want to train my model to be able to retrieve documents from a vector database. I want to go and take a look at benchmarks that have high scores on that task.

There is also the inference cost and latency. How fast is this model? Does it support multilingual and not only English? Lastly, the context length. How much text can I push in at once? Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed, mainly because we were very limited in the licensing part. Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family. These are Chinese family. Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies. Then we had to redo the whole work with models that are allowed. Both of them have great licenses. They are both open, even though I must say that comparing to Google, Nomic Embed by Nomic, they released it all. You are welcome to go and try. They released the training code, the model, the data. Anyone can reproduce the work. It's amazing. In terms of parameters or size, both of them are tiny, so it's great.

They are really fast. Context length, you can see that Google contains only 2K and Nomic Embed contains 8K. Google supports multilingual. If I go to best fit, then we decided, I have a choice now between Confluence, GitHub, and Jira. Now when we took a look at Google, they were very optimized for code search. We chose the EmbeddingGemma for code embedding. For Confluence, we decided we go with Nomic Embed because it has extensive technical documents it was trained on. Also, the context length gives us more flexibility when we want to embed things from Confluence.

Data Prep for Training

Going back to Confluence, I want to talk a little bit about, we decided now to fine-tune, now how do you start. You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning. We started with taking chunks, and I'm going to provide examples in the next slide. The chunking part, we did already in advance, so it was easy just to take the chunks we already handled. Then, step two, once I have one chunk, let's say, I'm taking an LLM to help me generate questions for that chunk. We generated three questions for each chunk, and of course, you can play with the number, that the chunks are supposed to answer those questions. This is how you generate, as you remember, the question and the positive document. Now, I would like to generate the negative documents. How do I do that? I have the questions, so we did a trick, and we took each question, and we went to the vector database, and we say, ok, let's take a model that wasn't trained, and retrieve documents from our vector database, but just, let's cap it so that the similarity when we retrieve is larger than 30%, but less than 80%.

We keep it in a range where the answer probably is not the most exact answer, but are not very far away. It's what we call hard negatives. They are answers that are not exactly answering what you ask, but they're not very far away, and we want to distinguish between those. We took the top 20, once you have 20 for the training, we kept 7 out of them. The number of negatives per training is just a parameter, and you can decide what to do. Then, you create triplets out of this process. How do you create triplets? That was a description of the process, so it's important you see one example in front of you, so a passage. We have to install Windsurf on Ubuntu WSL, just install. This is a chunk that we have. Now, I need to generate three questions out of it with an LLM.

As you can see, I generated three questions that are in purple, and the answers in green are exactly this identical chunk. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.

I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is important because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.

What would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.

Every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he said, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.

I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.

We go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.

This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.

Evaluation

This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we said that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.

Said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the new models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

Summary

I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.

Questions and Answers

Participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning, did you compare with providing the documents in the context? Without fine-tuning, did you use RAG approach by sending the related document to the model and getting the answers and comparing that with the fine-tuned embeddings?

Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. It's failing normally in specific areas when we have documents that are very specific to Dell, like product relationships and acronyms that are at Dell, this is where there were failures that we tested at the beginning. Again, when you have failures at RAG, and there are many, you ask yourself, ok, so it could be a problem of indexing, it could be a problem of the wrong chunking, there could be many things. This was one of the hypotheses, that it might be that the model doesn't understand the context, and we need to retrain.

Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?

Rachel Shalom: You are asking about like images, or attachments, or whatever. For different components, we did different things. For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. This is for tables. What else? Attachments. Attachments are PDFs, and PPTs, and all others are parsed and chunked as part of the chunking and embedding. After chunks, we embed it.

Participant 3: I have a question on fine-tuning. Why did you decide you have to find seven negatives, and how did you find those? Was it manual? Was it automated?

Rachel Shalom: How did I decide on seven negatives?

Participant 3: Yes, you mentioned that you have a question, you have one positive and up to seven negatives.

Rachel Shalom: The simple question is, I read the Nomic paper, and they used seven. I said, ok, they had a great success, so I'm going to take seven. That's the simple answer. The second answer is, I let Auto Research play also with the number of negatives, and see what happens to the loss. Auto Research reduced it to like zero or one, and then, your loss is amazing. I'm like, "Oh my God." I kept it seven, because I think I really carefully took a look at the paper, and I thought, ok, it makes sense. If we need to add more, we add more. I didn't plan to put less, because I think the more negatives you have, the better the training will be, but even more complex. I would retrain with different numbers in the next experiments. The basic answer is the paper.

Participant 4: Just to clarify, the fine-tuning workflow that you showed us was for an internal workflow at Dell.

Rachel Shalom: For internal data, you mean?

Participant 4: Or like, the embedding model is an internal embedding model.

Rachel Shalom: The embedding model is open source. It's called Nomic Embed. You can download it from Hugging Face. They released it together with the code, even. They have a bunch of beautiful code to train for different tasks, and the training data. I didn't use, obviously, the training data, but it's running on-prem at Dell. I didn't use any API, if that's what you're asking, to train it. Completely on-prem. I downloaded the model to Dell infrastructure and trained it there.

Participant 4: I was just wondering if you've benchmarked it with some other open-source models that are out there?

Rachel Shalom: If I was experimenting with others?

Participant 4: Yes.

Rachel Shalom: EmbeddingGemma, yes?

Participant 4: Yes, just like OpenAI text embeddings, or anything like that?

Rachel Shalom: The reason I didn't do it is because we are not allowed to send data to OpenAI.

entries.title: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload
entries.summary: Microsoft released .NET 11 with a .NET MAUI update focused on product quality. CoreCLR is now the default runtime on all platforms, and XAML gets incremental hot reload, implicit namespaces and faster resource dictionaries. The release also adds device test templates and passkey support, and raises the minimum Android and Apple platform versions. By Edin Kapić
entries.content:
Microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and new test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus.  Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

.NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

The runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with 

dotnet watch
, and can be disabled with 
EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload
. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root 
xmlns
and 
xmlns:x
are optional. Third, lazy 
ResourceDictionary
loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, 
RelativeSource
bindings with a resolvable 
AncestorType
now compile to trim-safe code.

Handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the new 

CollectionView2
handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for 
NavigationPage
, 
TabbedPage
and 
FlyoutPage
. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, 
Appearing
now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to 
NavigatedTo
.

Controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. 

TabbedPage
gains badges, 
BoxView
a 
Fill
brush, and 
LongPressGestureRecognizer
becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as 
trip/{tripId}
.

Animation methods now accept a 

CancellationToken
, and their non-
Async
variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a new 
Passkeys
class in 
Microsoft.Maui.Authentication
wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. 
Permissions.PostNotifications
now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

For Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

Several changes break existing code. The 

Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility
package no longer ships, the 
Color
record is now sealed, 
Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize()
is obsolete, and non-font 
SwipeItem
icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

The full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.
